column1: What should you inspect first in a punctuation question?
column2: Inspect the choices to identify the punctuation being tested. Then examine the relevant sentence structure. A candidate is correct only if it fits the whole sentence.

column1: What does CPIN stand for in the lesson?
column2: Colon; Period/semicolon/comma + FANBOYS; Isolated comma; No punctuation. Use it as a checking order, never as proof that a higher-priority choice is correct.

column1: What makes an independent clause?
column2: A subject and a finite verb expressing a complete thought: “The antenna receives signals.” A finite verb carries tense or follows a modal; an -ing word alone is not enough.

column1: Is “although the antenna receives signals” an independent clause? Why?
column2: No. Although makes it dependent. “The antenna receives signals” is independent; adding a subordinating word changes its status.

column1: Is “the antenna receiving signals from three satellites” a complete sentence?
column2: No. Receiving is a participle here. There is no finite main verb. “The antenna is receiving signals” is complete.

column1: How do you find the sentence skeleton when a subject is followed by extra information?
column2: Temporarily bracket a genuine nonessential insertion, then connect the subject to its main verb. “The antenna, installed last spring, receives signals” → “The antenna receives signals.”

column1: Can a comma alone connect two independent clauses?
column2: No. That produces a comma splice. Use an appropriate period, semicolon, or comma plus coordinating conjunction; a colon may work when the second part explains the first.

column1: When does a semicolon join clauses correctly?
column2: Both sides must be independent clauses. “The antenna failed; the team replaced it.” A fragment after the semicolon makes this use invalid.

column1: What are the two main semicolon jobs to check?
column2: Joining independent clauses and separating complex list items. In a complex list, the items do not need to be complete clauses.

column1: What does FANBOYS stand for?
column2: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So. When one joins two independent clauses, a comma usually comes before it. Check that the second part really has its own subject and verb.

column1: Does “and” automatically require a comma before it?
column2: No. “The team calibrated the sensor and recorded the results” has a shared subject and compound predicate. Do not insert a clause-separating comma merely because and appears.

column1: What must come before a colon used to introduce an explanation or list?
column2: A complete independent clause. “The team needed one tool: a wrench.” The material after the colon explains or specifies the statement before it.

column1: Must the material after a colon be an independent clause?
column2: No. It may be a word, phrase, list, or complete clause. “The team had one concern: overheating.” The left side must still be complete.

column1: Why is “The required tools include: a wrench and a drill” incorrect?
column2: The colon separates include from its direct objects. “The required tools include a wrench and a drill” is correct. Alternatively: “Two tools are required: a wrench and a drill.”

column1: Why is a colon not automatically correct between two complete clauses?
column2: The second part must explain, identify, exemplify, or expand the first. Mere completeness on both sides does not establish that relationship.

column1: How do you check a dash that closes an interruption?
column2: Locate the opening dash and identify the entire insertion. Use a matching closing dash when the main sentence resumes. Remove the insertion to verify the skeleton.

column1: Can a single dash introduce an explanation?
column2: Yes: “The team needed one tool—a wrench.” Do not assume every dash is one half of a pair; determine whether it introduces an ending explanation or encloses an insertion.

column1: How do you punctuate a nonessential phrase in the middle of a sentence?
column2: Usually with paired commas, paired dashes, or parentheses. Both boundaries matter. “The mural, restored last year, attracts visitors.” Do not mix an opening comma with a closing dash.

column1: Is “I can remove it and the sentence still works” enough to prove a phrase is nonessential?
column2: No. Removal must also preserve the intended identification and meaning. “The paintings that survived the fire were restored” limits which paintings; deleting the relative clause changes that claim.

column1: How are restrictive relative clauses usually punctuated?
column2: No surrounding commas: “The samples that remained dry were usable.” The clause identifies a subset. Restrictiveness is about meaning; the pronoun alone is not a complete test.

column1: What is wrong with “The researcher, published the results”?
column2: The comma splits the subject from its main verb. A real insertion can occur between them, but it must be enclosed: “The researcher, after checking the data, published the results.”

column1: When is a comma appropriate after a dependent clause?
column2: A dependent clause that introduces the main clause generally takes a comma: “Although the device was old, it worked.” A following integrated clause usually does not: “It worked because the team repaired it.”

column1: How do you punctuate a simple three-item list?
column2: Use commas between items: “The kit contains tape, string, and scissors.” On SAT-style questions, inspect the whole list before deciding what the blank separates.

column1: Why do some lists use semicolons?
column2: Semicolons make item boundaries clear when items contain internal commas: “Reno, Nevada; Albany, New York; and Boise, Idaho.” Keep each entire item together.

column1: How do you locate the semicolon in “Ada, a chemist; Leo, a physicist; and Mei, an engineer”?
column2: Each item is a person plus a description. The commas connect names to descriptions; the semicolons separate complete items. Match the repeated item structure.

column1: When does a profession directly before a name take no punctuation?
column2: When the profession and name identify a single person as one integrated unit: “Biologist Mara Chen spoke.” No comma goes between biologist and Mara Chen.

column1: Why can “Our only guide, Mara Chen, spoke” take commas?
column2: Our only guide already identifies a unique person in the stated context. Mara Chen supplies supplementary naming information. This is different from an integrated profession + name.

column1: How do you distinguish a direct question from an indirect question?
column2: “Where did the team work?” directly asks and takes a question mark. “The report explains where the team worked.” makes a statement and takes a period. Judge the entire sentence.

column1: Can “however” connect independent clauses with commas alone?
column2: No. Contrastive however is not a coordinating conjunction. Use “The model was simple; however, it was accurate” or “The model was simple. However, it was accurate.”

column1: How does punctuation change which clause “however” belongs to?
column2: “The model was simple, however; it was accurate” attaches however to the first clause. “The model was simple; however, it was accurate” attaches it to the second. Read the preceding sentence to locate the contrast.

column1: How can you tell whether “though” is a dependent-clause starter or a parenthetical transition?
column2: “Though the model was simple, it was accurate” begins with a dependent clause. “The model was simple, though; it was accurate” uses parenthetical though. Determine its grammatical role.

column1: If a period and a semicolon are both offered, can you always eliminate both?
column2: No. A semicolon may separate list items, a period may require a capital letter, and the choices may include other differing words. Substitute the complete choices and check the actual structure.

column1: If two punctuation choices both seem grammatical, what should you check next?
column2: Check capitalization, list boundaries, whether an insertion closes, and which clause a transition belongs to. Do not invent a stylistic preference to break a true tie.

column1: What should you say to yourself before submitting a boundary answer?
column2: “Left side: complete or incomplete? Right side: complete clause, explanation, insertion, or list item? What exact rule permits my choice?” Name the structural reason rather than relying on a pause.
